input.title: Forty-Two Fireflies and One Wrong Jar
input.openingPromise: Night has fallen on the festival bridge and the only light left in the valley is a glass dome swarming with 42 live fireflies. The bridgekeeper's cart waits to carry jarred light across, but the cart is picky: every jar must glow equally bright or the whole shipment tips. Pack the light right, or the valley goes dark.
input.firstThreeSeconds: A dark valley scene fades up; a glowing dome pulses with 42 drifting firefly sparks that softly illuminate the child's cursor. Empty jars slide onto a workbench with a gentle glass clink, and a light meter at the top of the screen begins a slow, visible drain. One firefly bumps the dome glass toward the nearest jar — an unmistakable nudge to start dragging.
input.firstAction: The child drags a jar from the rack onto the bench (jars snap into a row), then drags a scoop across the dome to pour fireflies into a jar. Each jar shows a live count and a brightness level; the very first drag produces glowing feedback within a second, no instructions to read first.
input.coreInteraction: A three-round packing instrument. The child controls two quantities physically: how many jars are on the bench (drag jars on/off the rack) and how many fireflies go in each jar (a scoop that pours in equal streams — pouring into one jar pours the same amount into all benched jars simultaneously, making equal-groups a mechanic, not a rule to remember). The cart's loading arm only lifts the tray when every jar holds the same count AND the dome is empty. Round 1: 42 fireflies, free choice among factor pairs (2×21, 3×14, 6×7, 7×6, 14×3, 21×2); the child commits, THEN the cart shelf slides open revealing exactly 6 slots — their arrangement is physically test-fitted against it in front of them; if it fails they must re-plan (repack) under a faster-draining meter. Round 2: 56 fireflies with the constraint stated up front on a wooden shipping tag: '7 jars, all equal.' The child must reason to the missing per-jar count; overfilled jars visibly overflow and half-filled jars sit dim, and escaped fireflies fly off into the night, permanently shrinking the swarm. Round 3: the bridgekeeper's handwritten order arrives: 'I need 9 lanterns lit tonight and each lantern eats 4 jars.' No total is given — the child must interpret that 9×4=36 jars of light are demanded, decide a packing from a dome of only 48 fireflies, discover the shortfall, and report it to the bridgekeeper by dragging the correct shortfall count onto the reply slate.
input.mathAsPower: Multiplication IS the packing machine. The equal-pour scoop makes jars×per-jar a lived structure: choosing 6 jars and pouring 7 rounds literally constructs 6×7 before the child's eyes, and the dome's live counter drains toward zero only when the product matches the total. Missing-factor reasoning is the only way to satisfy the shipping tag in Round 2 — guessing wrong causes physical overflow or dim jars, and the world punishes it by shrinking the swarm. In Round 3, interpreting the word problem correctly (compute 9×4, compare to 48) is the only way to know what to even ask the bridgekeeper for. Every multiplication decision changes brightness, jar count, cart acceptance, and the valley's light level; no answer buttons exist anywhere.
progression: Round 1 — The Free Pack (42 fireflies): open factor-pair choice; child commits an arrangement of their own design; the cart's 6-slot shelf is revealed only after commitment, forcing a test of re-planning versus re-running when a hidden physical constraint invalidates a mathematically valid answer. First arrangement, all reversals, and the child's spoken/typed reason are captured before the reveal.

Round 2 — The Shipping Tag (56 fireflies): constraint stated up front ('7 jars, all equal'); the child must derive the missing per-jar count of 8 — a fresh pair not in the rehearsed baseline; wrong pours cause visible overflow or dim jars and permanent swarm loss, and the light meter now drains faster after any spill.

Round 3 — The Bridgekeeper's Order (48 fireflies, total unstated): a written order ('9 lanterns, each eats 4 jars') requires interpreting that 36 jars are needed, packing what 48 fireflies can actually fill given a chosen per-jar amount, discovering the shortfall, and reporting the exact shortage on the reply slate — synthesis of all three skills with no rehearsed numbers (never asking 6×4=24, 5×6=30, or an answer of 7).

Escalating pressure across all rounds: the valley light meter drains continuously, drains faster after each spill, and the ambient scene visibly darkens — keeping total runtime near two minutes of real decisions.
input.visualDirection: Warm-dark palette: deep indigo night sky, amber-gold firefly glow, honey-colored glass jars with visible fill lines, weathered wood bench and cart. Every firefly is an individual drifting particle with a soft bloom halo so counts feel real and countable at a glance (jars auto-arrange fireflies in neat 1s/5s clusters inside the glass). The light meter is a lantern chain across the top whose lanterns gutter out one by one. The cart shelf reveal in Round 1 is a physical drawer sliding open with six carved slots — the mismatch (or match) is shown by literally trying to seat the jars. Overflow is theatrical but brief: lid pops, three fireflies spiral up and away, swarm counter ticks down. Readable at arm's length for a 9-year-old; numbers are large chalk-style digits on jar labels.
input.audienceRationale: A 9-year-old at ceiling on rehearsed multiplication needs the challenge moved off computation and onto decision structure. Direct manipulation (drag jars, pour equal streams) keeps the interface below his reading load while the constraint reveals carry the cognitive weight. The child evidence shows he finished a paced challenge fast, rated it 5/5, and moved on — so this design front-loads agency (free choice in Round 1), keeps rounds short and decision-dense (~2 minutes total), and makes each round structurally different rather than longer, matching a child who values brisk, complete-and-move-on experiences without assuming that observation is a durable preference.
input.stakes: The valley's night crossing depends on jarred light. Every spill permanently shrinks the swarm — fireflies that escape never come back this night — and the lantern-chain light meter drains in real time, faster after each mistake. If the meter empties before the order is resolved, the bridge goes dark and the festival team waits stranded on the far bank until the child re-lights the run.
input.consequences: Wrong arrangements are physically rejected, never verbally corrected: the cart arm strains, tilts the tray, and sets it back down if jars are unequal or the dome isn't empty; jars that don't fit the 6-slot shelf simply won't seat; overfilled jars pop their lids and lose fireflies for good; underfilled jars glow too dim to satisfy the shipping tag and the inspector taps the tag pointedly. Each spill accelerates the light-meter drain, so errors compound pressure without ending the run. In Round 3, reporting the wrong shortfall makes the bridgekeeper light the lanterns anyway — and the child watches the last lanterns flicker out mid-bridge, showing exactly how many jars short the report was.
input.recovery: Nothing hard-fails mid-round: jars can always be unbenched and re-poured (fireflies return to the dome, minus any spilled), so re-planning is always cheaper than repeating a failed commit. If the light meter empties, the round restarts with the same total but a fresh swarm and a slightly slower initial drain — the world forgives, but remembers: the bridgekeeper remarks on what went wrong ('The shelf holds six, remember'), turning the failure into a stated constraint for the retry. Round 3's shortfall report can be revised once before the bridgekeeper walks off.
input.payoff: On success, the packed cart rolls onto the bridge and the child watches their arithmetic become light: each lantern ignites from exactly the jars they packed, the bridge blooms amber across the water, and the festival team crosses. The Round 3 payoff honors honest math — correctly reporting 'we're short 3 jars' earns the bridgekeeper's respect and a torch-relay improvisation that covers the gap, making accurate shortfall-reporting the heroic act rather than a failure state. The celebration lasts no longer than the decision it follows: a single sweep of light, then the map.
input.replayVariation: On replay, totals and constraints reshuffle from a pool of multi-factor-pair totals (e.g., 36 with a 4-slot shelf, 40 with an 8-jar tag, an order of '7 lanterns × 6 jars' against a dome of 45), the hidden Round 1 shelf size changes, and whether the shortfall in Round 3 exists at all becomes uncertain — sometimes the dome exactly suffices, so the child cannot memorize 'report a shortage' as a script. Spill physics and drain pacing stay constant so mastery shows as faster, cleaner commits, not memorized answers.
input.motionDirection: Fireflies drift with gentle Perlin-noise wander and pour in smooth arcing streams that visibly split equally across benched jars. The cart arm's lift attempt is a slow, weighty ease-in that telegraphs success or strain before the verdict. The shelf-drawer reveal uses a deliberate 600ms slide with a pause — a beat of dread. Spills are fast (under 1s): lid pop, spiral escape, done. All celebration motion is a single 1.5s light sweep. No idle animations longer than 2s loops; the meter drain is continuous and smooth so time pressure is felt, not announced.
input.soundDirection: Ambient night bed: crickets, distant water, low festival murmur. Fireflies emit a soft granular shimmer that scales with jar fill — equal jars produce a consonant chord, unequal jars a subtle beating dissonance the ear catches before the eye does. Pouring is a gentle glass-and-chime cascade; a successful cart lift is a warm wooden creak resolving to a bell tone; a failed lift is a strained creak and a settle-thud. Spills get a quick pop and a fading flutter. The light meter drains silently until the last third, then adds a faint low pulse. No voice-over praise; the bridgekeeper's lines appear as written tags with a paper rustle.
input.worldReaction: The whole valley responds to the math: correct equal packing brightens the bench area and steadies the swarm's hum; each committed jar visibly dims the dome as its share leaves; spills darken the ambient scene a notch and speed the lantern-chain drain. The cart, shelf, tag inspector, and bridgekeeper each enforce constraints physically rather than judging verbally, so the child reads success and failure directly off the world's light, sound, and machinery.
input.engagementPrediction: Expected 2–3 minutes of high-decision-density play with at least one genuine re-plan event at the Round 1 shelf reveal. Prediction: the child commits quickly in Round 1 (consistent with prior brisk completion), experiences a productive surprise at the constraint reveal, and completes all three rounds without frustration signals; fun self-report ≥4/5; replay unlikely on first session but the reshuffled-total variation supports later revisits. Engagement telemetry: time-to-first-commit, number of reversals, spill count, meter state at completion.
input.falsifyingEvidence: The theory (transfer survives multi-factor-pair totals disambiguated only by physical constraint, with re-planning rather than re-running) is falsified if: (a) in Round 1 the child, after the 6-slot reveal, re-runs the same non-fitting arrangement or randomly cycles arrangements rather than converging on 6×7; (b) in Round 2 the child pours by trial-and-error increments rather than committing near 8-per-jar, or repeatedly produces rehearsed-adjacent counts (6 or 7 per jar) despite the stated tag; (c) in Round 3 the child packs without computing the demanded total, or reports a shortfall unrelated to 36−48-derived reasoning. Captured evidence: the pre-reveal Round 1 arrangement, every commit/reversal timestamped, the child's stated reason at each commit, and the Round 3 interpretation path (whether 9×4 was constructed before packing).
input.interactionContinuity: One continuous physical grammar across all three rounds: drag jars to bench, pour equal streams, commit to the cart. Rounds change only what the world demands (hidden constraint → stated constraint → constraint to be inferred), never how the child's hands work, so all cognitive escalation lands on the math and none on relearning controls. The swarm, meter, and bridgekeeper persist across rounds as one unbroken night.
input.interactionDemonstration: Worked example of Round 2: the tag reads '7 jars, all equal' with 56 fireflies in the dome. The child benches 7 jars. Pouring one scoop cycle adds 1 firefly to each jar simultaneously (dome drops by 7 per cycle, visibly). A child reasoning 7×?=56 commits to 8 cycles and pours confidently; the dome empties exactly as the eighth cycle completes, jars chord in consonance, the cart lifts. A child guessing pours past 8 — on cycle 9 the dome is empty mid-pour, jars are unequal, lids strain; or stops at 7 cycles and the inspector taps the tag at 7 dim jars with 7 fireflies still circling the dome. The mechanic itself makes the missing factor tangible: cycles-of-7 is the multiplication, and the dome counter is the running product.
usefulLibraries: PixiJS (WebGL particle rendering for hundreds of glowing firefly sprites with bloom)
GSAP (drag interactions, cart-arm and drawer easing, meter tweens)
Howler.js (layered ambient bed, pitch-scaled jar shimmer, pour and spill SFX)
matter-js (optional light physics for jar seating and lid-pop spill arcs)
